title: The US Is About to End a 30-Year Student Visa Rule. No Country Has More at Stake Than India.
excerpt: A proposed rule eliminating 'Duration of Status' would cap F-1 stays at four years, slash grace periods, and threaten the Day-1 CPT pathway that thousands of Indian graduates depend on.
body:
The most consequential change to the American student visa system in three decades is heading for the finish line — and Indian students are squarely in its crosshairs.

On May 5, the Department of Homeland Security submitted its final rule to the Office of Management and Budget, moving to eliminate what's known as "Duration of Status" for F-1 student visas. The rule, proposed in August 2025 and expected to take effect as early as September 2026, would replace the open-ended system that has governed international students since 1979 with a rigid four-year cap — after which students would need to apply for formal extensions through USCIS.

For the roughly 300,000 Indian students currently in the US — who make up one of the largest international student populations in the country — the implications are sweeping.

How the System Works Today

Under Duration of Status, international students on F-1 visas are admitted for as long as they maintain valid student status. There is no fixed expiration date stamped on their I-94 arrival record. Extensions, program changes, and transitions to Optional Practical Training are handled through the student's university, not through the federal bureaucracy.

This flexibility has been the backbone of the Indian student pipeline for decades. A student can extend their program, switch majors, or begin OPT without filing a single application with USCIS.

What Changes Under the New Rule

The proposed framework would fundamentally restructure this system. Every F-1 student would be admitted for a fixed period — the length of their program, capped at four years. Anyone who needs more time, whether for continued studies, OPT, or STEM OPT extensions, would have to file a formal Extension of Stay application with USCIS.

The rule would also cut the post-program grace period from 60 days to 30 days, giving graduates less time to secure employment sponsorship or transition to another visa category. And crucially, it would apply retroactively to students already in the country.

"The duration of status rule that has been proposed is going to fundamentally change the flexibility that students have had to apply for Optional Practical Training and Curricular Practical Training," said Danielle Goldman, co-founder and CEO of Build, an immigration advisory firm.

The Day-1 CPT Pathway Under Threat

For Indian graduates who fail to win the H-1B lottery — a scenario that plays out tens of thousands of times each year — the most common fallback has been "Day-1 CPT" programmes. These allow graduates to enrol in a new academic programme while continuing to work legally through Curricular Practical Training.

The new rule would make this pathway significantly narrower. Graduate students would be prohibited from changing programmes at any point, and extensions would not be granted to students pursuing a second degree at the same or lower level as their first.

"For anyone who already has a master's degree, they are not going to be able to go back and say, 'I need another master's degree because I need work authorisation to continue working,'" Goldman said.

Why India Is Hit Hardest

The numbers are stark. Indians account for approximately 48% of all OPT and STEM OPT participants in the United States — roughly 79,000 on STEM OPT alone, according to ICE data. They also receive over 70% of all approved H-1B petitions annually.

This structural dependence on the F-1-to-OPT-to-H-1B pipeline means any disruption ripples through the entire Indian student community. H-1B approvals for Indians have already dropped 37% in the current fiscal year compared to FY2024, a combined effect of the wage-weighted lottery and the $100,000 employer fee introduced last September.

A 2025 survey by NAFSA and the Institute for Progress found that 54% of current international students would not have chosen the US if OPT were not available. If the new rule makes OPT extensions more cumbersome and uncertain, the impact on Indian enrollment could be substantial.

The Employer Squeeze

Goldman warned that the ripple effects would reach well beyond students. US companies, particularly in AI, machine learning, and software engineering, rely heavily on international talent. Foreign nationals make up a substantial portion of the US AI talent pool.

"There's no doubt about it that this is going to have a massive impact on the companies that are in desperate need of top talent," Goldman said. "The companies will either struggle because they won't have the talent or they will have to get creative and find alternate solutions."

Some employers may turn to cap-exempt H-1B programmes or O-1 visas for highly accomplished professionals. But for the vast majority of Indian graduates entering the workforce through standard channels, the options are narrowing fast.

What Happens Next

The final rule is now with the Office of Management and Budget for review. NAFSA, the leading international education association, has said the administration wants the rule in place for students arriving in the fall 2026 semester, which would require publication by late June or July.

The public comment period closed in October 2025. Over 30,000 comments were submitted, the overwhelming majority opposing the change. But the administration has shown little indication it plans to retreat.

For Indian families weighing whether to send their children to American universities, the calculation has fundamentally changed. The US is no longer just competing on the quality of its education — it's now asking students to bet on a system that may not let them stay long enough to use it.
